anomaly_def.Name: Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly + Storage Space Capacity Anomaly + Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
Transaction Log Subsystem Anomaly : The log-writer, flush, and archiver pipeline cannot keep pace with redo generation, driving up commit-path latency.
Storage Space Capacity Anomaly : Physical or logical free space for data, log, archive, temp, or backup areas is exhausted, preventing further allocations and recycling.
Network and Connectivity Resource Anomaly : Network transport or connection-handling resources are saturated or unstable, delaying client traffic and any log shipping or archival flows.

When these three root causes strike at once, the database faces a compound failure on its primary write-commit path, on-disk capacity, and on the network channels that move log and archive data. Observable symptoms intertwine: commits and checkpoints stall while log flush waits soar; log switches trigger but hang because the next segment cannot be created on a full device; archiver or replication processes report timeouts or disconnections as congested networks throttle log shipping; free space in both active and archive log destinations plummets, producing "cannot allocate log" or "out of space" errors; meanwhile clients experience connection establishment delays, query timeouts, and sudden disconnects as socket queues overflow and retransmissions spike. The administrator may see a rapidly growing queue of unarchived log files, a surge in retry storms from application tiers, and an overall degradation that is hard to attribute to any single layer.

Causally, heavy transactional activity first drives up log-write volume. Because archival throughput is limited by network congestion, completed log segments linger, consuming space in the log/ archive area. As capacity is consumed, the storage subsystem rejects further extensions, blocking new log switches and forcing foreground transactions to wait for space. The prolonged commit latency keeps connections open longer, increasing session counts and network load, which further stresses already constrained listener and socket resources. The feedback loop—log saturation → space exhaustion → blocked archiving → network retries → additional log growth—amplifies itself until the database enters a near-hang or shutdown condition. Only coordinated remediation of log tuning, space reclamation/expansion, and network bandwidth or connection-handling limits can break the cycle.

entry.official_definition: Specifies the amount of time after which a TCP keepalive message that has not been acknowledged by the client should be retransmitted.
entry.trigger_condition: A TCP keepalive probe is not acknowledged for tcp_keepalives_interval on systems supporting TCP_KEEPINTVL or an equivalent socket option.
entry.workload_impact: Controls retry timing for keepalive probes used to detect unresponsive client connections.
entry.default_behavior: Default value is 0, selecting the operating system default.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when connection establishment, authentication exchange, or session activity does not progress within the allowed time budget.
entry.solution_guidance: Check connection lifecycle, client responsiveness, authentication latency, idle-session handling, and whether connection pools are holding stale sessions.
